idiom_name: struct with function-typed fields implementing the interface
implementation_notes: Go's structural interfaces plus first-class functions collapse the classic configurable double into a struct whose fields are the collaborator's methods as function values; each test sets only the functions it cares about and the double satisfies the interface as long as the fields' signatures match the methods. No framework or code generation is involved, the double can be narrowed to the small interface the SUT actually consumes, and testify's mock package is the toolkit alternative when interaction assertions and argument matchers are wanted. The struct form is still the honest default because a hand-written fake is three lines and needs no dependency.
pitfalls: A nil function field panics only when the SUT calls that method, so an unconfigured fake fails deep in the code under test instead of at setup; initialise every field with a function that fails the test or returns the zero value.
A value-receiver struct is copied when passed as an interface, so recording calls in a field needs pointer receivers or a pointer to the recorder.
Fakes that outlive one test (package-level) keep their configured closures, which is the Go version of leaked double state.

variants.name: gomock generated mocks with EXPECT().Return()
variants.implementation_notes: mockgen generates a MockX type from the interface in source, package or archive mode; the test creates a controller with gomock.NewController(t), configures each call with m.EXPECT().Bar(gomock.Eq(99)).Return(101) (or DoAndReturn for answers computed from the arguments) and the controller fails the test when an expectation is unmet or an unexpected call arrives. The generated file is the statically generated configuration interface, and testify's embedded mock.Mock is the reflection-based alternative when code generation in the build is unwanted. Prefer generated mocks once interfaces are wide or when call-count and argument-matching assertions are central; keep the generated mock in step by regenerating it from go:generate.
pitfalls: Generated mocks drift from the interface unless mockgen runs in the build; a stale mock keeps compiling and hides the change.
The controller is bound to a testing.T-like reporter, so a mock used from a helper goroutine or a subtest needs the matching controller or it reports against the wrong test.
DoAndReturn callbacks run on the caller's goroutine; a callback that calls back into the same mock or blocks on a channel the SUT also waits for deadlocks the test.
